creditSources.title: Source for the displayed object and recorded credits

studyData.intro: Four planes are enough for this deliberately spare lower-volume paperback: green field, title, volume marker and author. Look at how a narrow red column carries several kinds of information without introducing another illustration.

regions.label: Opening title characters
regions.summary: The first characters begin a vertical path.

sections.heading: Read down the central column
sections.body: The title begins ノルウェイ, the Japanese rendering of Norway. Its katakana characters are stacked vertically, so a reader follows the column downward rather than scanning a horizontal title across the cover.

sections.heading: Space around a thin red path
sections.body: The column occupies little of the cover’s width. Large green areas on both sides allow the red strokes to remain prominent without bold borders, pictures or a second competing block of text.

regions.question: What directs your first movement more strongly: the red colour or the vertical arrangement?

regions.label: The title’s lower words
regions.summary: The column changes character shapes as it descends.

sections.heading: Norwegian Wood
sections.body: The complete title is ノルウェイの森, commonly published in English as Norwegian Wood. The lower の森 continues the same column, bringing a curved hiragana character and a denser kanji form into the sequence of katakana above.

sections.heading: Different densities in one line
sections.body: The characters do not all occupy the same amount of red area. The dense strokes near the title’s foot form a stronger local cluster than some of the more open characters above, producing variation within an otherwise simple arrangement.

regions.question: Which character looks darkest when you step back from the cover?

regions.label: Circled lower-volume marker
regions.summary: A small sign distinguishes this part of the book.

sections.heading: The lower volume
sections.body: The circled 下 identifies the lower or second volume in this two-part paperback presentation. It is smaller than the surrounding name characters, but its circular boundary gives it a distinct role within the vertical column.

sections.heading: Selecting the correct volume
sections.body: Kodansha’s record identifies ISBN 9784062748698 as the lower volume of the 2004 paperback. The small marker therefore helps a reader choose the intended part; it is useful publication information, not merely an ornamental punctuation mark.

regions.question: Could a reader overlook this marker if it used the same size and spacing as the title?

regions.label: Vertical author name
regions.summary: A second name continues below the volume sign.

sections.heading: Haruki Murakami
sections.body: 村上春樹 is the author’s name, read Murakami Haruki in Japanese name order. It is arranged vertically beneath the volume marker, keeping authorship within the same central route while distinguishing it by position.

sections.heading: A quiet continuation
sections.body: The author line uses the same red as the title rather than introducing a new accent. The small gap and intervening volume sign do the separating work, so the cover maintains a single colour relationship throughout its wording.

regions.question: How do position and spacing tell you that this is a new piece of information?

regions.label: Broad green field
regions.summary: Most of the cover remains green.

sections.heading: A large uninterrupted colour area
sections.body: The left side contains no large illustration or additional text. Subtle surface variation remains visible within the green, but it does not interrupt the overall impression of a broad field around the thin red column.

sections.heading: Emphasis through restraint
sections.body: Because so much of the surface remains quiet, the small amount of red can command attention. This is a relationship between area and contrast: increasing the red text’s width would also change the apparent scale of the surrounding green.

regions.question: How much of the cover could remain green before the title began to feel too small?

regions.label: Red against green
regions.summary: The shared text colour makes separate roles belong together.

sections.heading: One warm printed colour
sections.body: Title, volume marker and author all use a red-pink hue against dark green. The contrast is visible throughout the column, although fine stroke edges reflect the limitations and texture of the reproduction rather than a perfectly clean vector outline.

sections.heading: Unity without identical meaning
sections.body: A shared colour makes the three verbal groups feel related, while spacing and the circled marker distinguish their functions. The design demonstrates that information does not need a separate colour for every category to remain organised.

regions.question: If the author changed to white, would the column feel more legible or less unified?

regions.label: Room above the wording
regions.summary: The title does not touch the top edge.

sections.heading: A small breathing interval
sections.body: Green remains visible above and around the first title character. That margin gives the opening stroke a defined position within the object rather than making it look cropped by the edge of the reproduction.

sections.heading: A beginning without a frame
sections.body: The cover does not use a top rule or coloured panel to announce where reading starts. The first isolated red stroke and the remaining green margin establish that beginning through placement alone.

regions.question: Would moving the first character closer to the top make the design feel more urgent?

regions.label: The specific paperback surface
regions.summary: The work’s date and this object’s date differ.

sections.heading: 2004 cover, 1987 work
sections.body: Kodansha identifies this lower-volume paperback as published on 14 September 2004. The novel first appeared in 1987; the displayed object is therefore dated 2004 rather than being presented as the original hardcover simply because the work is older.

sections.heading: An unverified design credit
sections.body: The consulted product record does not establish a separate designer credit for this displayed cover. Its visual restraint can be described precisely without attributing the arrangement to a named person or claiming a particular printing technique.

regions.question: Why should a catalogue distinguish the date of a novel from the date of the cover being shown?
